roundtrip.frame: 操作 2/3 · 已测试水格 (1,1)，候选面积 4 · best（已编号岛及已测候选最大值）= 4 格
roundtrip.derive: 对一个水格 z，seen 是它四个方向中不同的陆地编号集合。新岛面积 A(z)=1+Σ area[k]，k∈seen。集合会把重复编号合并。邻接同岛两次不会创造新陆地；不接触 z 的岛也无法经唯一的新陆格进入这个岛。

roundtrip.title: #827 Making A Large Island
roundtrip.frame: Operation 2/3 · Tested zero (1,1), candidate area 4 · best (completed islands and tested candidates) = 4 cells
roundtrip.derive: For a water cell z, seen is the set of distinct land IDs among its four neighbors. Its new island has area A(z)=1+Σ area[k], for k∈seen. The set merges repeated IDs. Touching one island twice adds no new land; an island not touching z cannot enter the new island through the single added cell.

Accumulate possible arrival lengths

How can we avoid enumerating routes without losing a possible crossing? R[x] is the set of possible previous jump lengths on reaching coordinate x; a set merges duplicate lengths. Start with R[0]={0}. This artificial 0 is not a real jump: only 1 among candidates −1, 0, 1 is positive, enforcing the required first hop.

A separate algorithm simulation, not execution of the Python below. Cards are ordered by coordinate; spacing does not represent river distance. Each shows x and the discovered R[x]; ∅ means no arrival discovered yet. The orange border marks the source just processed. Changing a preset resets this simulation. Each “Process next state” checks all three candidates for one (x,k), retaining discovered sets and operation history.

Keep the default preset and advance through (3,2). Observe R[3]={1,2} and R[6] changing from ∅ to {3}; go back to remove that addition. The source is one possibility being expanded, rather than the frog’s only actual position.

Not finished; the last stone’s current set is ∅. A nonempty set already proves reachability; an empty set does not yet prove failure.

Cumulative operation history

Why trust these sets? An invariant is a statement that stays true after every operation: every k in R[x] has a legal route witnessing it; once all stones before x are processed, R[x] contains exactly all legal arrival lengths. The artificial initial (0,0) is valid. Each addition comes from a witnessed (x,k), uses a positive permitted length and lands on a stone, so it invents no route. Conversely, the last hop of any real route comes from a smaller coordinate; that predecessor was processed, so its arrival length must be added.

Every move goes forward, so updates write to later stones and never change the source set being iterated. One pass in increasing coordinate order suffices. At the end, the last set is nonempty exactly when a crossing exists. The diagram stores history snapshots for undo; the submission does not.

03

Search by layers

How can the first encounter with the goal prove the fewest moves? Breadth-first search (BFS) explores one move count at a time. The frontier contains every newly discovered state at distance d; seen is the set of all discovered states. The start is layer 0 because no move has been made.

Keep 123405: 0 occupies position 4 (zero-based, row-major), so it can swap only with positions 1, 3, 5. This gives 103425, 123045, 123450, each reachable in 1 move. The last is the goal and layer 0 was not, so the answer is 1. Later, when 103425 generates 123405, seen rejects it: that board was already found at layer 0, and returning cannot improve its distance.

This yields the invariant: on entering layer d, the frontier is exactly the states whose shortest distance is d, and seen is exactly those within distance d. One edge from the frontier reaches a state within d+1 moves. An unseen state cannot be within d moves, or it would already have been discovered. Its distance is therefore exactly d+1. Mark it seen immediately to avoid duplicates within the new layer. Every (d+1)-move path has a penultimate state within d moves, so the next layer misses no state either. This proof relies on every edge costing one move.

Word Ladder II: retain shortest paths by layer →

Finish “One move”, then select “Five moves”. Advance layer by layer and inspect the retained layer ledger. Each frame shows the full frontier on entering that layer. The candidate ledger details the previous layer’s first state; all other states were also fully expanded. Changing the preset restarts this search.
